Maricopa County bills it, not the city. The Maricopa County Assessor decides each parcel's value and classification. The Maricopa County Treasurer sends the bill and collects for more than 1,800 tax districts, including the state, county, cities and towns, schools, community colleges and special districts, then passes the money on.

That gives a Phoenix owner two offices, each with its own set of questions.

  • Assessor: the value on your Notice of Valuation, your home's legal class, appeals, notices of claim and personal exemptions. It sits at 301 W Jefferson St, Phoenix, AZ 85003, and the appeals line is 602-506-3406.
  • Treasurer: the amount due, payment options, refunds, delinquent notices and tax lien information.

Phoenix sets its own rates but doesn't assess your home or collect from you. Its share shows up as a single line on the county bill.

The tax comes due in two halves, October 1 and the following March 1 (A.R.S. 42-18052). A half turns delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on November 1 or May 1. When that date is a weekend or holiday, the deadline slides to 5:00 p.m. on the next business day.

The slide applies in 2026. November 1 was a Sunday, so the first half of 2026 became delinquent after 5 p.m. on Monday, November 2, and an unpaid first half is now late. May 1, 2027 is a Saturday, so the second-half deadline should roll to Monday, May 3, 2027.

Late tax carries 16 percent a year in simple interest, and a fraction of a month counts as a whole month (A.R.S. 42-18053). No interest is collected on a full-year payment made by December 31 of the tax year, so with the first half of a 2026 bill unpaid, you have until Thursday, December 31, 2026 to pay both halves and avoid it. A bill of $100 or less is due in one payment on October 1 and turns delinquent after December 31.

Phoenix had an estimated 1,665,481 residents in July 2025. Among the city's 15 urban villages are Ahwatukee Foothills, Camelback East, Laveen, Maryvale, Encanto and South Mountain. Recent figures show 57.3 percent of homes owner-occupied and a median owner-occupied home value of $420,700.

One city holds very different housing, and the school, community college and special districts on your bill depend on the parcel. A home in Maryvale and one in Ahwatukee Foothills share a city but not necessarily a tax bill. Look up your parcel on the Assessor's site to see which districts apply, since two houses a mile apart can have different total rates.

For 2026-27 the city's published notice proposed a primary rate of $1.2652 per $100 of assessed valuation, slightly down from $1.2658, and a secondary rate of $0.7745, down from $0.8141. The city said that even with the lower primary rate, rising assessed values would still lift primary taxes for the average owner by 2.79 percent. Call the Treasurer for the rates now in effect.

Primary and secondary tax pay for different things.

  • Primary tax supports General Fund services such as police and fire, parks and recreation, libraries and community centers. State law limits how fast a city's primary levy can grow (A.R.S. 42-17051).
  • Secondary tax pays bonded debt service for facilities such as libraries, police and fire stations, storm drains and parks.

Those are only the city's rates. Your county, school district and community college add theirs, so your bill is higher than the city line. Maricopa County posts rate and levy tables for every taxing jurisdiction on its Tax Levy and Rates page.

Send a petition to the Maricopa County Assessor within 60 days of the date your Notice of Valuation was mailed (A.R.S. 42-16051). Notices arrive in late winter, so read the mail date printed on yours and count 60 days from it.

The Assessor's appeals page separates three filings, and choosing the wrong one costs time.

  • Real property appeal: for a belief that the full cash value or classification is wrong. File the Petition for Review of Valuation (AZDOR Form 82130R) by mail or in person. Emails aren't accepted for real property appeals.
  • Notice of Claim: for a factual error such as wrong square footage. It reaches the current year and the three prior years, and an approved claim can produce a refund through the Treasurer.
  • Residential Legal Class Change: for a home that became your primary residence. Your name and the property address must appear on a driver's license, voter registration, or a tax return address page plus a vehicle registration or utility bill.

Bring evidence to any of them. Appeals with no documents, such as appraisals or comparable sales, may be denied.

The Assessor's Valuation Relief division runs personal exemptions for widowed owners, totally disabled owners and veteran owners. Applications are due by February 28, or by September 1 with an approved Exemption Deadline Waiver. Every program requires Arizona residency and household income under the statutory limit.

  • Widowed or totally disabled: up to $4,873 off the limited property value.
  • Veteran with a service-connected disability under 100 percent, or a nonservice-connected disability: up to $4,873, multiplied by the disability percentage.
  • Veteran with a 100 percent service-connected rating: the primary residence is fully exempt when every requirement, income included, is met.

The income cap is $39,865 for households with no children under 18, and $47,826 where children under 18 or disabled children lived in the home the prior year. Social Security, military pensions and VA disability payments don't count as income. Call 602-506-3406 before applying, because buying or selling property can end eligibility.

Clear any unpaid tax before or at closing. A county treasurer can sell the lien for all delinquent taxes on a property together, not just one year's (A.R.S. 42-18104). Have your title company pull the balance and put it on the settlement statement.

A few steps keep closing on schedule.

  • Ask the title or escrow officer for a payoff that includes interest through closing day.
  • If the first half of 2026 is still open, interest has been running since November 2.
  • If you recently paid off a mortgage, ask the Treasurer about the interest waiver in A.R.S. 42-18053(C). It covers a delinquency within one year after a mortgage or deed of trust is released, needs board of supervisors approval and can be used once per property.

The deed is recorded with the Maricopa County Recorder. Staff there can't give legal advice or fill in documents, and there is no notary service. The recording services line is 602-506-3535. All of this works the same whether the buyer pays cash or uses a loan.

faqs.q: Does the city of Phoenix collect my property tax?
faqs.a: No, Maricopa County does. The Assessor sets value, and the Treasurer bills and collects, including the city's share. That share is one line on the county bill.

faqs.q: What is the last day to pay 2026 Phoenix property tax without interest?
faqs.a: December 31, 2026, for the full year. Under A.R.S. 42-18053 no interest is collected on a full-year payment made by December 31 of the tax year. Paying only the first half after November 2 leaves interest running on the unpaid half.

faqs.q: What interest applies to late Maricopa County property tax?
faqs.a: Sixteen percent a year, simple, from the delinquency date until paid, with a partial month counted as a whole month. The treasurer, with board approval, may waive interest once per property for a delinquency within a year after a mortgage is released.

faqs.q: Can I appeal my Phoenix home value?
faqs.a: Yes, within 60 days of the mail date on your Notice of Valuation. Wrong square footage or another factual error is handled by a Notice of Claim, which can reach back three prior tax years.

faqs.q: Must I pay the tax before selling my Phoenix house?
faqs.a: Clear it before or at closing, with interest in the payoff. The Maricopa County Treasurer or your title officer can give the exact figure for your parcel.
